text:
The public relations staff were excellent and very helpful. The doctor was smiling and kind, but the wait time was very long because the doctor spent a considerable amount of time with each patient. The lab nurse who dressed the wounds had a grumpy expression, seemed in a bad mood, and spoke harshly and unpleasantly. I took an 86-year-old to get their wounds dressed, and when they bowed to the nurse, she was very sullen and didn't smile at all. The next day, when I asked something politely and respectfully, she responded irritably and gave a lengthy explanation. Couldn't she explain things without getting upset? She's working in public service, receiving taxpayer money. If she doesn't want to care for patients, she should take on administrative tasks that don't involve interacting with people. Years ago, I met a kind, lovely, and humble wound dressing nurse; I wish they would bring that person back.

The wound dressing queue was empty. I arrived at around 7 am but was given queue number 46. I waited for over an hour and still hadn't been treated. The nurses in the lab were idle because the medical records department is terrible; they don't separate wound dressing patients' records but combine them with the general patient system, which has a queue of over 60 patients, while they only see less than 10 patients per hour.

text: There were a lot of people, mostly elderly. The nurses were very patient. The elderly who couldn't hear well spoke loudly, but not in a shouting manner. However, the wait was long. Just for the tetanus shot, I waited 2 hours because I had to wait in line to be called to take a medical history and see the doctor together with general cases. They should really be separated because it only takes a few seconds to be called, but the wait to be called in is very long.

The dental clinic... I took my son there to have a tooth extracted... I understand that extraction might cause the tooth to become crooked... but they should have done something else... I mean, scaling, because the school checkup also …
Every time I come, I'm never disappointed. The doctor is kind and gives good advice to patients, and all the nurses provide excellent service.

text:
I took my cat to get vaccinated, but they didn't even give me a missing cat sign. They told me to put it somewhere people couldn't see it. The next day, they took off the sign and put it outside the health center instead. They couldn't even give me a sign? Don't they have any compassion?

Do the staff still have any humanity? Or do they love this rotten government agency? Is it so off-limits to the area? Why is it so much of a problem just to put up a sign?

A friend had her cat vaccinated here, and the cat got lost there a few days ago. The vaccination was done in an open area, and it was said that vaccinations could be done in cars. However, the officials were hesitant because no one would catch the cat, so they brought it to the pavilion to vaccinate. The cat ran away and disappeared, and no one took responsibility. Until now, it has not been found. The owner has been looking for it every day. Pets are like family. Please be considerate. We are a service center for the public.

The way they spoke to their friend was very unpleasant and they showed no responsibility whatsoever for the missing cat. I'm very confused. Employees really shouldn't speak to customers like that, for example, saying "This area is full of snakes." Who owns the cat? One cat is missing, and we can't even put out a missing cat announcement anymore. No one is okay with being spoken to like that again.

Vaccinating dogs and cats against rabies is free, but shouldn't there be a closed room for providing the service? Dogs and cats escape, and no one takes responsibility. The area is almost entirely forested. When they suggested vaccinating …
Good service, all the staff are lovely, and the place is clean.

This is a clear double standard in queuing. The blood test queue is combined with the general treatment queue, making the patient care process disorganized. It would be better to separate the queues – blood tests in one queue and general treatment in another – to avoid confusion.
